first_impression.reaction: I'm a corporate lawyer, not a family lawyer, and James's parents are contributing a fair bit, so the prenup question has come up. I googled it to get the basic shape before we raise it properly. The intro gets straight to it: what it's called, when you can sign it, and that you both need your own lawyer. No hearts and rings rubbish. Good enough to keep going, mostly to find the bit about marrying overseas.

journey.quote: As at November 2026, it is only binding if it meets the technical requirements of the Act, and each of you must receive independent legal advice from an Australian lawyer before you sign.
journey.reaction: Correct, dated and to the point. That's the sentence I'd want my non-lawyer friends to read first.

journey.quote: The celebration itself is where [Wedded Concierge](https://weddedwonderland.com/wonderland-concierge?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=prenup&utm_content=primary) comes in.
journey.reaction: It's a bit early to plug a planner in the third paragraph of a legal explainer. Not pushy, but it makes me wonder whether the article is really about the prenup.

journey.section: Why some prenups are set aside
journey.quote: [Victoria Legal Aid](https://www.legalaid.vic.gov.au/agreement-about-dividing-property) says financial agreements are legally binding unless it can be proved that: there was fraud; the agreement is not practical; it did not follow the formal requirements under the Family Law Act; there has been a major and unexpected change affecting a child; one person acted in an unfair way; one person did not follow the agreement; or property covered was taken by the government because of criminal activity.
journey.reaction: Two long lists of set-aside grounds back to back, saying mostly the same thing. And the independent legal advice point has been made about five times by now. I started skimming here.

journey.section: Who needs a prenup? Couples it often suits
journey.quote: No source says a couple needs one.
journey.reaction: I like the honesty that it's our call, but 'no source says' reads like someone's research notes, not something written for me.

journey.section: Couples living or marrying across countries
journey.quote: An agreement made overseas is not automatically recognised in Australia and must meet the Australian formal requirements to be valid here.
journey.reaction: This is the kind of thing I was actually looking for. If we marry in Europe, I would not want to sign anything locally on the assumption it counts at home. Useful.

journey.section: How to get a prenup and when to sign before the wedding
journey.quote: talk to your lawyer early, well before the final weeks fill with fittings, flights and seating plans.
journey.reaction: Fair and practical. Nobody wants to be signing this in the same fortnight as the seating chart.

journey.section: Prenups for destination weddings and international couples
journey.quote: If you plan to sign in Australia and then marry overseas, ask your lawyer how the overseas ceremony affects your agreement.
journey.reaction: That's exactly our situation and the page just hands it back to me. I get that they can't give legal advice, but at least give me the questions to take into the first meeting so I don't pay for an hour of figuring out what to ask.

journey.section: Prenup after marriage: is it too late?
journey.quote: If your circumstances have shifted since you signed, a new house, a child, a move overseas, raise it with your lawyers rather than assuming the old document still fits.
journey.reaction: Sensible. Not for us now, but it's a good honest line.

journey.quote: Your Wedded Advisor plans the venue, travel and vendors with you, with the fee agreed in writing before any work begins.
journey.reaction: Fee in writing before any work starts is the line that matters to me. Calm close, no hard sell.

unanswered_questions: If we sign a prenup in Sydney and then marry legally overseas, what are the questions we should bring to our first lawyer meeting?
Is it better to marry legally in Australia first and have a celebration abroad, from a prenup point of view, or does it make no difference?
Roughly how far ahead of the wedding should we start, so it doesn't land in the last month?
Does a Wedded Advisor ever coordinate with a couple's lawyers on timing (for example, around a legal ceremony abroad), or is that entirely on us?
would_share_with: James: the 'Couples living or marrying across countries' and destination sections, because they change how we think about a legal ceremony abroad
Not the parents. It's a conversation for us and our lawyers first.

cta_reaction.why: It's honest that the agreement stays with the lawyers and they handle the celebration. But I came for legal basics, not inspiration. I might click to look around; I wouldn't enquire off this post. I'd want a couple more posts and a real wedding first.

top_3_changes: In 'Why some prenups are set aside', merge the Legal Aid NSW and Victoria Legal Aid lists into one short list, and stop restating the independent legal advice point in every section. By the middle I was skimming the same facts twice.

In 'Prenups for destination weddings and international couples', replace the bare 'ask your lawyer' with a short list of general questions a couple could take to their first meeting (signing here then marrying abroad, assets or family overseas, timing against the wedding date). Still general information, but it gives me something to do.

Rewrite 'No source says a couple needs one.' in plain reader language (for example, that nobody has to have one and it's a decision for the two of you), and consider dropping the Wedded Concierge link from the intro so the legal section reads as genuinely helpful before the planning pitch.
